title: Your season now
hookLine: name your current season: Scholastica asks her brother Benedict for one more night, and a storm answers
tomorrow: a monk begged the Buddha to write rules. why did the Buddha wait?

lines: SHE PRAYS, AND THE SKY BREAKS.
cards: Saturday morning, and the plan says one thing while someone you love needs another. Benedict knew that pull. His sister Scholastica, a nun, comes to visit him at a house near his monastery.
Brother and sister, both given to God, in one house. They spend the day praising God and talking. Night falls.
Stay, she says, let's talk until morning. He refuses: a monk sleeps in the monastery. So she folds her hands on the table, bows her head, and prays.
And the clear sky breaks open: thunder, lightning, a downpour so heavy no one can step outside.

teach.h: I ASKED MY GOD, AND HE LISTENED.
teach.b: God forgive you, sister, Benedict says. What have you done? She answers: I asked you, and you wouldn't listen.
I asked my God, and he listened. So they stay up through the night, talking of holy things, until morning comes.
Gregory the Great, who tells the story, explains it simply: she could do more, because she loved more. Within days, he says, she died. Here's the teaching, and it's written into Benedict's own Rule.
A rule of life isn't one timetable forever.
The Rule sets one schedule for summer and another for winter, with different hours for work and reading, and a pattern of its own for Lent. Even the meal times move with the year.
Benedict wrote a rule that expects the year to turn. The rule bends to the season, and on one stormy night, Benedict bent to love.
So, today's question: what's your season? Student, householder, someone midway, someone stepping back, someone caring for the old?
A rule written for a different season will chafe. Name the season, and let the rule fit it. Benedict's Rule has room for that.

how: The Rule of Benedict sets different hours for work, reading and meals in summer, in winter and in Lent. Benedictines remember Scholastica, Benedict's sister, through Gregory the Great's story of the storm.

o: the weather where you live this time of the year
the sports season your favorite team is playing
naming the stage of life you're in, so your rule fits

s: the Rule of Benedict keeps one timetable all year round
it sets different hours for work and reading in summer, in winter and in Lent.
in Gregory's story, Scholastica's prayer kept her brother through the night
a storm broke from a clear sky, and they talked until morning.

games.q: your friend's rule says a morning run, every day. she just had a baby and is furious at herself for "failing." what fits Benedict's Rule?
o: name the new season and let the rule fit it; Benedict kept summer and winter hours.
keep the morning run no matter what; a rule that bends isn't a rule.
drop the rule entirely; a new season means no practice at all.
games.why: the Rule of Benedict moves its hours with the year, and Gregory's story puts love above the timetable. A rule fits its season.

practice: Say your season in one word, quietly: student, builder, parent, midway, stepping back, caregiver, or a word of your own.
Then pick one line of your rule that doesn't fit this season, and decide how it bends: a different hour, a shorter form, a new place. Sit with that choice for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Your season now: naming the stage you're in, so your rule can fit it, the way Benedict's Rule kept summer hours and winter hours, and gave Lent its own.

orig.note: Latin: she could do more, who loved more. Gregory's line about Scholastica.

carryVoice: Here's the line: my season, a Rule that moved with the year, and love that outranked the clock on a stormy night. Day 1688, season named.

sources.ref: Gregory the Great, Dialogues 2.33-34 (Scholastica visits Benedict at a house near the monastery; she asks him to stay the night; he refuses; she prays and a storm breaks from a clear sky; 'I asked you and you would not listen; I asked my God and he listened'; she could do more because she loved more; her death soon after)
